title: Seven Hammer Clangs Taught a Baby Fear, Yet Half of Textbooks Got Little Albert Wrong
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Watson & Rayner (1920): 'Little Albert', the Claw-Hammer Steel Bar & History's Most Controversial Fear Test, grounded in John B. Watson, Rosalie Rayner (1920) (Journal of Experimental Psychology). Empirical findings show that at 8 months, 26 days old in late 1919 at Johns Hopkins, 'Albert B.' was filmed on a white nursery mattress reaching out calmly with ZERO fear toward a tame white rat, a rabbit, a dog, cotton wool, masks, and even burning newspaper.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Only ONE stimulus triggered an unconditioned startle reflex in Albert: Watson standing behind the infant's back and striking a suspended 4-foot-long, 3/4-inch steel bar with a carpenter's claw hammer.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- John B. Watson, Rosalie Rayner (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069608
- Russell A. Powell, Nancy Digdon, Ben Harris, Christopher Smithson (2014). Correcting the record on Watson, Rayner, and Little Albert: Albert Barger as “Psychology’s lost boy”. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0036854
- Nancy Digdon, Russell A. Powell, Ben Harris (2014). Little Albert’s alleged neurological impairment: Watson, Rayner, and historical revision. History of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037325

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
